source: Accounts at a Glance 2024-25, Office of the Principal Accountant General (A&E), Andhra Pradesh, drawn from the state's certified Finance Accounts.
audit_source: CAG State Finances Audit Report No. 2 of 2024 (year ended 31 March 2023), the latest state finances audit the CAG has published for Andhra Pradesh.

flags.title: Central scheme money with no bills
flags.plain: The state passed central and state scheme money to its own implementing agencies. The auditors never received the bills or vouchers showing how that money was actually spent.
flags.why: Without bills, nobody outside those agencies can confirm the money reached the works and people it was meant for.
flags.kid: Like giving someone money to buy books and never seeing a receipt.

flags.title: Cash advances never accounted for
flags.plain: Officials drew 202 cash advances for expenses but had not submitted the bills by 31 March 2025. Rules give them 90 days. 85 of these advances are more than a year old.
flags.why: An advance with no bill is money whose use is unknown. The auditors warn this carries a risk of misuse.
flags.kid: Officials took money in advance and did not show what they bought.

flags.title: Loans given without any conditions
flags.plain: The state lent this money without writing down the interest rate, repayment period or other terms, as its own rules require. ₹251.78 crore was paid to different companies than the borrowers it was approved for.
flags.why: Loans without terms may never be repaid, and the public cannot tell who owes what.
flags.kid: The state lent money without writing down when it must come back.

flags.title: Borrowing kept out of the budget
flags.plain: This much was owed through borrowing done by state companies on the government's behalf. The budget did not show how much or from where.
flags.why: It does not appear in the budget, but taxpayers still have to repay it.
flags.kid: Money borrowed through state companies, so it doesn't show in the main budget.

flags.title: Spending put in the wrong categories
flags.plain: Spending was recorded under the wrong headings. For example, ₹1,981.54 crore of electricity bills was listed as small construction works.
flags.why: It makes the state look like it spent more on building lasting assets, and less on running costs, than it really did.
flags.kid: Electricity bills were written down as building work.

flags.title: Unused scheme money sitting in bank accounts
flags.plain: Scheme money was lying unspent in agency bank accounts at the end of the year. None of it was returned to the central government.
flags.why: Money meant for schemes that sits idle is help that did not reach people.
flags.kid: Money meant to help people sat unused in bank accounts.

flags.title: A loan recorded as tax income
flags.plain: In March 2025 the state liquor corporation sent this money to pay NTR Bharosa pensions, as a short-term loan. It was recorded as excise tax collected.
flags.why: It makes the state's tax income look bigger than it was.
flags.kid: Borrowed money was written down as tax the state earned.

flags.title: Grants with no proof of use
flags.plain: When the state gives a grant, the receiver must send a utilisation certificate showing how it was used. The auditor could not even find out how many certificates were missing, because the grant orders were never sent to it.
flags.why: In the auditor's words, the possibility of fraud or misappropriation cannot be ruled out.
flags.kid: Nobody knows how many 'here's how I spent it' letters are missing.
